look_here_first: PURPLETOP: look for a widely OPEN and usually drooping flowering panicle on a comparatively tall perennial. The archived purple photograph and pale old-head photograph prove that color is variable. Bare proximal portions of branches occur in BOTH purpletop and Texas tridens; verify a true short hairy ligule and mature spikelet/lemma characters.

morphology_keys.family_pattern: Poaceae: use growth habit, ligule, panicle architecture, spikelet form, lemma hairs and awns. For this old Tridens complex, panicle openness/color and current genus placement are especially useful.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: By far the tallest and most visibly purple member of this batch. The broad reddish-purple panicle separates it quickly from the narrow white seedhead of T. albescens.
field_sequence: 1. Look at the base: multiple upright culms from a tufted perennial crown, often about 60–180 cm tall, with overlapping somewhat flattened lower sheaths.
2. Pull back a leaf blade and inspect its inner collar: ligule is a SHORT FRINGE OF HAIRS, about 0.5 mm; the collar often has additional hairs. No projecting auricles.
3. Measure a leaf blade where possible: usually 3–10 mm wide, flat and tapering; leaf color or white midrib alone is not proof.
4. Check a mature head: an airy, pyramid-shaped open panicle with branches often bending/drooping at the tips; spikelets often purple or reddish, occasionally yellow.

5. With a hand lens, check multi-flowered spikelets (often about 5–10 mm) rather than the tiny one-flowered spikelets of redtop bentgrass. Note sticky/oily mature panicle branches as supporting, not sole, evidence.
morphology_keys.diagnostic_warning: Purple color is seasonal and shared by other grasses; inspect the hairy ligule and multi-flowered spikelets before assigning this species.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Against T. texanus, don't use bare lower panicle branches as unique: both species have them; compare total spread, culm size and measured glumes/lemma. Against T. albescens, widely open flower-bearing branches versus tightly appressed contracted branches are strong first clues. Purple is not required: this second source photo is straw-colored.

field_matrix.look_alike: Often a medium-sized perennial bunchgrass with a tight, lance-shaped upright panicle (Kew ~8–25 cm); appressed branches carry crowded green-to-white/purplish spikelets. Both existing photographs show this distinctly. Compare with purpletop's open head and Texas tridens' flexuous exposed branches. Check nearly equal glumes and restricted lemma-nerve hair distribution under hand lens; current photos are habit only.

field_matrix.look_alike: Perennial grass commonly 20–75 cm with a panicle often about 5–16 cm: slender flexible lateral branches can have long empty lower sections, ending in prominent often pink/rose spikelets with 6–12 florets. Existing mature arching photo and close-up both show these gross characters, but purpletop can have the SAME bare branch feature. For real ID compare the mature glumes about half lemma length and lemma-nerve hairs below midlength; avoid relying on rosy color, panicle droop or bark/soil habitat alone.

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: Large perennial with broadly open, many-branched, often nodding panicle (commonly 15–35 cm). Red/purple spikelets in bloom frequently mature dull tan; the two local pictures demonstrate both phases. Compared to Texas tridens, purpletop tends more expansive and larger but panicle lengths overlap; both can show exposed branch bases. Check flattened basal sheaths, short hair-fringe ligule, mature lemma nerve hairs, and possibly sticky panicle branches rather than treating stickiness or color as a mandatory ID.

measured_diagnostic_key_20261022.look_here_first: PURPLETOP: seek a tall perennial tuft with a large open, often nodding panicle, then confirm multi-flowered spikelets and a very short hairy/ciliate collar. Purple pigment and exposed basal branch lengths are NOT exclusive species tests.

measured_key.growth_form: Perennial with firm knotty shortly rhizomatous base; culms approximately 60–180 cm in FNA treatment. Record actual rooted basal crown.
measured_key.ligule_collar: Ligule a very short ciliate membrane or hair fringe, up to about 0.5 mm; collar conspicuously hairy. Do not mistake the longer collar hairs for the true ligule.
measured_key.panicle: Open panicle approximately 15–40 cm, with widely spreading or drooping branches, often naked along lower one-third to one-half; these bare branch bases also occur in T. texanus.
measured_key.spikelet_glumes: Pedicellate spikelets 5–10 mm with commonly 4–8 florets. Two one-veined awnless glumes: lower about 2.5–3 mm, upper about 3.5–4 mm.
measured_key.lemma_palea: Fertile lemmas approximately 3–5 mm, three-veined, two-toothed at tip; fine hairs along veins especially lower portions; midvein may project to about 0.5 mm as a mucro. Palea nearly lemma-length.
measured_key.awns: No true long awns. Minute projecting lemma midvein (to about 0.5 mm) must not be annotated as a long awn.

measured_diagnostic_key_20261022.local_lookalikes: T. texanus may share pink spikelets and naked lower branch segments but generally has smaller, more flexuous flowering panicle; confirm mature glume/lemma dimensions and nerve hairs. T. albescens has much narrower, contracted, upright panicle; panicle color alone fails.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Tridens flavus — first recognize the head, then verify spikelet parts
steps: See the first SOURCE-LABELLED PHOTO: use gross branches and spikelets as starting clues, not independent expert taxon confirmation.
Compare second photo to learn variable maturation/color/branch posture.

NEW ACTUAL MACRO: see intact multi-flowered purpletop spikelet at right of Matt Lavin's licensed photo, and separate pieces on left/center. These are real pixels, not proven labels for individual glumes/lemmas; compare real specimen under 10–20×.
At 10–20× on a real ripe specimen, remove a spikelet and measure the paired outer GLUMES against a fertile LEMMA.
Examine hairs on the 3 raised LEMMA NERVES; this is a principal separation, but no current photo proves it.
Check 0.2–0.5 mm hairy ligule/collar and basal sheath on the SAME rooted plant; leave tentative Tridens sp. if reproductive anatomy absent.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Species-level Tridens confidence requires panicle architecture PLUS mature spikelet/glume/lemma anatomy; do not identify from pigmentation alone.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Bare panicle branch bases are not unique to Texas tridens. Source-labelled photos do not establish unreviewed county nativity.
